meta.note: Week 44 is the latest FPA report with machine-readable text at retrieval time. Weeks 45-46 (Nov 2-13, 2026) are posted as scanned images; update these numbers from the FPA weekly-prices page before the demo if needed. A dash in the FPA table (no data) is stored as null.

Nitrogen(N).label: Nitrogen deficiency
Nitrogen(N).symptoms: Older (lower) leaves turn pale yellow-green, starting at the tip; the whole plant looks light green, short, with few tillers.
next_steps: Check several plants across the field, not just one leaf. N deficiency usually shows on the older leaves first and across the whole field.
Compare leaf colour with a Leaf Color Chart (LCC) or PhilRice's Leaf Color Computing app to confirm and estimate how much N is needed.
Ask your Municipal Agriculture Office (MAO) or use the MOET kit / Rice Crop Manager for the right amount and timing for your field.
N is usually top-dressed in splits (for example at early tillering and at panicle initiation) rather than all at once.
Nitrogen(N).fertilizer_notes: Urea (46-0-0) is the most concentrated N source. Ammosul (21-0-0) also supplies sulfur. Complete and Ammophos are usually used as basal fertilizer and also add P (and K for Complete).
Nitrogen(N).wrong_prediction: If the leaf is not really N-deficient, extra urea can cause lush, weak growth, lodging, and more pest and disease problems, and excess N can wash into water. It also wastes money that should go to the nutrient that is actually missing.

Phosphorus(P).label: Phosphorus deficiency
Phosphorus(P).symptoms: Plants are stunted and dark green with narrow, short, upright leaves and few tillers; leaves may have a reddish or purplish tint.
next_steps: Look at the whole plant: P deficiency shows as stunted, dark green, upright plants with few tillers more than as spots on one leaf.
Confirm with a soil test (DA Regional Soils Laboratory) or the PhilRice MOET kit before buying fertilizer.
P works best when applied early (basal or at early tillering); late P has little effect on this season's yield.
Ask your MAO for the right rate for your soil and target yield.
Phosphorus(P).fertilizer_notes: DAP (18-46-0) is the most concentrated P source. Ammophos (16-20-0) and Complete (14-14-14) supply P together with N (and K for Complete).
Phosphorus(P).wrong_prediction: The model's most common error is between P and K. If the leaf is really K-deficient, P fertilizer will not fix it: the K problem continues, yield is lost, and the money for DAP or Ammophos is wasted.

Potassium(K).label: Potassium deficiency
Potassium(K).symptoms: Older leaves have yellowish-brown or orange margins and tips, with rusty brown spots that spread; plants may be dark green and stunted.
next_steps: Check older leaves on several plants for brown or orange leaf edges and tips. K symptoms are often clearer after panicle initiation.
Because K and P can look alike in photos, confirm with a soil test or the MOET kit before buying fertilizer.
K is often split: part at planting (basal) and part at early panicle initiation. Returning rice straw to the field also adds K.
Ask your MAO for the right rate for your soil and target yield.
Potassium(K).fertilizer_notes: Muriate of potash (0-0-60) is the most concentrated K source. Complete (14-14-14) supplies K together with N and P.
Potassium(K).wrong_prediction: About 1 in 10 'K' results on the test set were really P deficiency. If that happens, potash will not fix the problem: the P deficiency continues, tillering and yield suffer, and the money for MOP is wasted.
